analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies federal land from logging, mining, and drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill gathered 72 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, but never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would designate large areas of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, wildlife corridors, and recovery areas. It would ban new road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas development that damages the roadless character of those lands, and it would let federal agencies accept ranchers' donations of grazing permits to retire them. It also directs a panel of independent scientists to evaluate remaining roadless forests and creates restoration jobs repairing damaged land.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use and depend on public lands: hikers, hunters, anglers, and the downstream communities and farms that rely on clean water from the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other river headwaters. The bill's findings argue that taxpayers also benefit because they currently subsidize timber sales that return less than they cost [S3]. Outdoor recreation businesses and local restoration contractors would gain work. Future generations gain a permanently protected wild region supporting endangered wildlife like grizzly bears, wolves, and caribou [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Designates federal lands across five states as wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, biological connecting corridors, and wildland recovery areas, permanently shielding them from development [S2] [S3].

Prohibits new road construction, timber harvest, oil and gas leasing, mining, and other development that impairs the natural and roadless qualities of evaluated roadless lands, unless Congress later acts [S2].
Lets the Interior Department and Forest Service accept donations of grazing permits and leases, giving ranchers a voluntary way to retire grazing on sensitive public lands [S2] [S3].

Directs federal agencies to develop wildland recovery plans and establishes rehabilitation zones with restoration work, which the bill's findings say would provide contracts for local businesses [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber, mining, and oil and gas industries, which would lose access to roadless federal lands they can currently log, mine, or lease. Counties and rural communities that depend on timber jobs and timber-related revenue would bear an economic cost, and users of motorized recreation would lose access in newly designated wilderness areas [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation permanently bars motorized recreation, road building, and most commercial development, including timber harvest, in the designated areas, an irreversible loss of access for loggers, miners, off-road users, and the counties that collect revenue tied to those activities [S3].

The bill acknowledges that rural, resource-dependent communities have faced economic instability and high unemployment from overexploitation of these lands; replacing timber jobs with seasonal restoration work is a real transition risk for affected towns [S3].

It is a large, top-down designation drafted primarily by members from outside the region, leaving affected western states with permanently fixed federal land rules that only a future act of Congress could change [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades permanent, irreversible restrictions on resource extraction for permanent protection of water sources, wildlife habitat, and recreation for the public, with taxpayer savings from ending below-cost timber sales [S3]. The costs fall on a small set of industries and on some rural communities whose economies would need to adjust; the benefits are spread broadly across the public but are harder to see day to day. The permanent, one-way nature of the designations is the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act on March 10, 2021, with 43 original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S5].

The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction, and on May 12, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands and the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples of the United States [S5].
The bill accumulated 72 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, including Rep. Raúl Grijalva, chair of the committee where the bill sat [S4] [S3].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place; the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still stuck at the subcommittee-referral stage [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies kept their access to roadless federal lands in the Northern Rockies, and no member had to take a recorded vote on the protections. Recreational users, downstream water users, and wildlife gained nothing, since the lands remain open to development under existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support; the bill was referred to subcommittees on May 12, 2021, and Democrats, who controlled the House, never advanced it to a hearing or a vote [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill bans timber harvest on designated lands and restricts it on evaluated roadless lands, ending an extraction the bill says taxpayers subsidize through below-cost sales [S2] [S3].
Mining that impairs the natural and roadless qualities of evaluated lands is prohibited, closing off potential new mine sites on federal land [S2].
Oil and gas leasing is prohibited on evaluated roadless lands and development is barred from designated wilderness and recovery areas [S2] [S3].

Existing grazing rights are respected, but agencies must accept voluntary donations of permits for retirement, giving ranchers a paid exit option while gradually reducing grazing on sensitive lands [S2] [S3].
Permanently protected wild lands and rivers sustain the hunting, fishing, and wilderness-based recreation economy the bill describes, along with restoration contracts for local businesses [S3].
